title: Why Norris has committed to McLaren for the long term
excerpt:
Michael Jordan and Scottie Pippen, Xavi and Andres Iniesta, Lando Norris and McLaren – there are just some sporting partnerships that are meant to be.

On Saturday, it was announced that the latter will be staying together for the foreseeable future with Norris signing a fresh deal that'll keep him at McLaren until at least the end of 2030.

When Zak Brown got to know a young aspiring racer called Lando Norris, very quickly he formed the opinion that the Briton was World Championship material.

Brown was proved right last year as the 26-year-old fended off team mate Oscar Piastri and a charging Max Verstappen to clinch the Drivers' World Championship crown.

That title success came in year nine of their time together, which began with Norris walking through the doors of the McLaren Technology Centre (MTC) in Woking in 2017 as a 17-year-old to sign a contract to become test and development driver.

Norris was an instant hit with McLaren and McLaren was an instant hit with Norris. They've grown up together, gone through tough times together and enjoyed success together. They've got each other's respective backs.

That's the kind of environment that Norris thrives in. As he told me in his first interview since the news broke, he's with the people that he wants to be with and "for me, that's calming".

Norris' previous contract ran until at least the end of 2027, so there was no rush to get a new deal done, not least because both Brown and Norris knew they were happy and wanted to continue. So why do another deal already?

Well, following his World Championship victory last year – McLaren's first Drivers' World Championship trophy since Lewis Hamilton triumphed in 2008 – it was always the plan to sit down and discuss extending and improving their arrangement.

Norris signs new McLaren deal until end of 2030

So, in the last few months, they zeroed in on the new terms with both sides sure that, not only did they want to continue beyond 2027, but they wanted to commit for the long-term, which in this case is at least the next four years.

The deal is understood to be a proper commitment from both sides and a clear intention to see it through, rather than a deal that has clauses that could allow one or the other to escape each year.

For Norris, he was keen to do a long-term deal to give him and those around him stability and prevent the persistent rumours about his future floating around and acting as a distraction.

Knowing he'll be at McLaren untll at least the end of 2030, when he'll be 31, also means he can knuckle down and focus on working with his team to add to his win and World Championship tally.

He also believes McLaren have what it takes to win. He believes Brown and Team Principal Andrea Stella are "incredible" leaders and feels the team of people who work with him are the best in the business and are all working in the right direction to bring success. So there really was no reason to change.

For McLaren, they have seen Norris grow from a rising star to a World Champion and were there every step of the way, from signing his first contract and taking his first pole, to sealing his first Grand Prix win and taking the title.

They know what they've got – and they know what he's worth – so understandably, they don't want to let him go.

Signing such an impressive deal that locks him down for at least another four years gives certainty to their shareholders and partners and wards off any admirers – of which there are many – elsewhere in the pit lane.

The driver market could get very spicy in 2028, so locking Norris down early doors sets out their stall and sends a warning signal to rivals.

Trust and belief in each other. Those factors formed the foundations of Norris and McLaren's relationship back in 2017 and, a decade on, they remain the cornerstones.

With team mate Piastri signed up until the end of 2028 – and both sides believed to be very happy with their relationship – McLaren are well set for the future as they battle to create a papaya-coloured dynasty in the years ahead.

title: Norris opens up on why he sees his future at McLaren
excerpt:
Lando Norris is beaming. This isn't uncommon as it's pretty much his baseline, but the Briton's smile and chirpiness is noticeably even brighter when we meet on the uber-cool boulevard of the McLaren Technology Centre for a chat.

This is because Norris is here to talk about a huge new deal that will keep him at McLaren until at least the end of 2030. Come the end of that term, he'll have been with the team for 12 years, equaling the record stint countryman Lewis Hamilton had with Mercedes.

It's an extraordinary show of faith in McLaren, with the British team holding the same belief in Norris. And given how perfect Norris and McLaren seem for each other, it's perhaps no surprise that he's chosen to extend his stay with a team where he feels at home.

"I'm very, very excited," he says in his first interview since the news was announced. "McLaren's been my home since the very, very beginning of my career in Formula 1 and I want it to stay that way for as long as possible. We've had a great few years and I'm confident we can achieve that many more times. So I want to stay."

Norris began his F1 journey with McLaren, starting as a test and developing driver, before stepping up as a reserve. He got the nod for a race seat in 2019, racing alongside Carlos Sainz, and went on to take his first podium in Austria 2020 and first pole in Russia 2021.

His first win came in Miami 2024, his first Monaco triumph in 2025 and his first Grand Prix victory on home soil followed that year when he won at Silverstone. He of course would go on to pick up his first World Championship and McLaren's first drivers' title since 2008.

They've seen it all together but they're not done yet. Why change what isn't broken? Especially when you can confirm your long-term future and give yourself some stability.

"I know for a good amount more years that I'm comfortable in terms of I've got a job and I’m where I want to be, and with the people that I want to be with, and for me that's calming," he says. "I can focus on a job I need to do and as a team we can also focus on the job that we want to do."

He adds: "You can always see results as most important and 99% of the time I think they are, but I would say there's leeway, there's leverage in terms of just the fact I'm with the people that I want to be with, people that I enjoy spending my career with.

Norris signs new McLaren deal until end of 2030

"I don't want to be bouncing around teams and doing different things. I want be where I'm happy and, even when we weren't winning, I was also happy to be part of McLaren.

"I think something I always know for my future is I want results of course – the team know that just as much as anyone – but I also just want to be wherever I'm most happy and even if we're not winning like the beginning of this year, it's not like I want to change team.

"I'm still very happy with who I am with and happy to kind of fight through whatever we have coming up."

'I don’t want to distract my team'

Fighting back McLaren are. After a slow start, which included McLaren failing to take the start in the opener in Australia and both failing to start at the following race in China, the reigning World Champions are fighting back.

An upgrade in Hungary before the break hauled them into contention and opened the door for Norris to secure his and the team's first victory of the season. That package was completed with more parts after the break in Zandvoort, with Norris taking pole and a second successive victory.

He's still someway off in the championship fight, as he sits 83 points behind leader Kimi Antonelli, but he and McLaren have the momentum – and if last year is anything to go by (when Max Verstappen sliced through a 104-point deficit to force a title decider in Abu Dhabi) Norris is very much in with a chance of defending his title.

That response is just what Norris knows McLaren are capable of, but that form didn't trigger this renewal. Those chats had been in the diary since he won the world title in Abu Dhabi last year.

Norris knew he wanted to stay and McLaren knew they wanted to keep them. To warn off admirers from elsewhere on the grid and to stamp out any ambiguity about his future, they were both keen to extend.

Drivers' Championship after Zandvoort

"It's a continuation of my last [contract]," he says. "We just want to be able to focus on doing our best job, to extract performance, to get the most out of everyone and focus on the importance that we do not get caught up in the mess of everyone else deciding contracts.

"I don’t want to distract my team, I don't want to distract the guys and girls here that are here to give me the best car possible and for me to do the best job for them.

"We want to focus on our jobs and not think about all the noise that goes on in the sidelines. So for me it's 'guys I'm here to stay. I want to be with you for a long time' and it gives them a good boost, gives me a good boost and together it means we can just focus."

'I want to make this my home'

Norris also believes in the set-up McLaren have, led by CEO Zak Brown and Team Principal Andrea Stella. "Zak is a very good leader, he's a very good boss," says Norris.

"As much as we get on and we just, we love racing, we want to win together, we enjoy golf and things, he is still my boss so he still gives me a kick whenever I do something wrong or if I'm not doing something well enough.

"That's always what I want – someone that's honest and who gives me the brutal truth no matter what it is and that something that's very important to me.

"At the same time I have that very much so with Andrea, and Andrea is for me – and of course I'm biased and this is the only place I've been – but we have had a few different team principals and he is most certainly the most influential over the team.

"He is an incredible leader, someone who knows how to bring a group of people together and also knows how to lead individuals such as me in terms of how I can go out and increase my performance every day and be a better person.

"So, even if I could change anything with where I am now, I wouldn't and I think that's the perfect reason."

Will Norris, who will be 31 when this next deal expires, ever leave McLaren? There's a very good chance he won't.

"I want to make this my home," says the Briton, who holds the record for the most starts for McLaren. "I want it to be the place that I am at for a very, very long time and maybe even forever.

"There are more nice things that just allow me to work better here and live better here, and that's an amazing thing."

title: Norris signs new McLaren deal until end of 2030
excerpt:
Lando Norris has committed his future to McLaren after signing a new deal that will extend his stay at the British team until at least the end of 2030, with a multi-year option to commit beyond that date.

The Briton joined McLaren in 2017 as a test and development driver before earning promotion to the grid as a race driver for 2019.

The 26-year-old has since gone on to claim 13 Grand Prix victories, 18 pole positions and 48 podiums – as well as his maiden World Championship in 2025. Additionally he has now raced in 163 Grands Prix for the team, more than any other McLaren driver in history.

His previous deal is believed to have been set to expire at the end of 2027, but McLaren moved to lock him down for the foreseeable future with a fresh contract extension.

As well as confirming his future, Norris will also be gifted an MCL39 by the squad, which he raced during his title-winning season last year.

“McLaren is my home, and I’m very pleased to be signing a new contract to keep me with the team until at least 2030," Norris said.

"When I started this journey nine years ago, I was clear about the goals I wanted to achieve: to get McLaren back to the front and to win championships. We’ve achieved that goal, but we want more, we want to keep on winning, and we know as a team that we’re capable of achieving it.

"I can’t wait to get back in the car in Monza and I’m very excited about what the future holds for us, both over the rest of this season, and in the coming years.”

McLaren CEO, Zak Brown, said: “I’m incredibly pleased to be signing a new contract with Lando, extending his commitment with McLaren until at least 2030. His journey with the team is a fantastic example of our commitment to identifying, developing and supporting world-class talent, and his achievements speak for themselves.

"Together with Andrea [Stella], Oscar [Piastri] and the wider team, Lando has helped drive McLaren into a new papaya era of success, helping us go from the back of the grid, to double consecutive constructors’ titles in 2024 and 2025 and our first Drivers’ Championship in 17 years. We are extremely excited about what lies ahead and remain fully focused on continuing to compete for wins and championships.”

McLaren Team Principal, Andrea Stella, added: "Lando has been an integral part of McLaren’s journey and success over the last nine years, and we are delighted to continue our partnership with him through to at least 2030.

"He is an exceptional driver, someone who combines outstanding natural speed with maturity, consistency and a strong commitment to McLaren, but above all, he is a special human being who is valued by everyone in the team.

“Since joining McLaren as part of our junior programme, he has grown with us and played a central role in bringing the team back to the front of Formula 1. This extension gives us important continuity and reinforces our confidence in the direction we are taking together.

"With him and Oscar, we know we can count not only on one of the strongest partnerships but also on one of the most united and close-knit teams in Formula 1.”

By the end of the current agreement, Norris will be 31 and have spent 12 years with McLaren, matching the stint Lewis Hamilton achieved with Mercedes.

His deal expires at the same time as his rival and friend Max Verstappen, who recently committed to Red Bull, whom he joined in 2016, until the end of 2030.

Norris' team mate Oscar Piastri, meanwhile, is contracted with McLaren up until the end of 2028, having signed a fresh deal ahead of the 2025 campaign. That gives McLaren stability for at least the next two Formula 1 campaigns.

title: Why Aston Martin is bringing house music to F1 fans
excerpt:
Earlier this week, Aston Martin announced a partnership with British record label and house music specialists Defected. The pairing of motorsport and music is nothing new, but with a huge growth of fans in both F1 and house, the collaboration feels like it’s coming at just the right time.

House music as a genre was born in Chicago at the start of the ‘80s and has only grown in popularity, becoming mainstream with tracks frequently populating the global charts.

It’s already got a presence in Formula 1; just take a look at a driver’s social media round-up and you’ll likely see it paired to a house tune – yes, Oscar Piastri, we’re looking at you.

Aston Martin have taken this to another level with their partnership with Defected Records, hosting a ‘Driven By Sound’ pop-up in Central London for their I/AM members. From the outside, this pairing might feel like an interesting choice, but it’s a collaboration that makes a lot of sense.

“We want to associate ourselves with iconic properties and Defected absolutely ticks that box,” Rob Bloom, Aston Martin's Chief Marketing Officer explained.

“Defected is the belief that house music exists on and off the dance floor, and that community culture is so much more than just the music. We are absolutely in that mindset as the Aston Martin Formula 1 Team, and we want to engage fans and welcome them into our world, whether you go to a Grand Prix or not.

“The Aston Martin brand is 100 years old, but it's always been a cultural phenomenon. It existed way beyond its core product, we are very comfortable – in culture – punching outside of category, and that's the space we play, in which we are so much more than just a car company or motorsports team.”

How Alonso used a unique strategy to earn P9 in Zandvoort

Music has always had links with Formula 1, from its association with ‘The Chain’ by Fleetwood Mac to the incredible album created for F1 The Movie – the two passions always find a way of coming together. However, with so many genres to pick from, why did Aston Martin gravitate towards house?

“There's a natural alignment," Bloom continues. "If you look at house music and F1, we both bring scale and intimacy. Two global properties, in house music and Formula 1, and there are 825 million F1 fans out there in the world: it's truly global.

"But, when you bring fans together at little moments like this, that's where you get the intimacy. You can have huge global platforms that still have very intimate personal relationships and experiences as part of it.”

For Aston Martin's I/AM members, the Soho pop-up is a great chance to get up close and personal to the team, with activations that include a complimentary coffee whilst enjoying DJ sets from Sam Divine and RUZE, or a run club that’s hosted on the Sunday.

Once inside the venue, there’s also plenty to see: from Fernando Alonso’s race suit and helmet to a sound wall which invites guests to listen to a mix of team radio, the Honda power unit and team radio from their F1 ACADEMY driver Mari Boya.

“Dance music has evolved a lot since I've been doing this,” said Simon Marlin, a house producer from The Shapeshifters. “There's nothing more unique than finding friends on the dance floor.

"Defected Croatia is a great example of people that had never met each other 10 years ago, and now are the best of friends, crying with each other because the festival finished this year.

"That can only happen through shared experiences that are delivered in a way that makes you feel special, that makes you go beyond what you expected. They're the moments that bring people together, and house music is the biggest and best platform to do that. It's such a feel-good factor.”

The exploration of house music in Formula 1 has been seen through the genre’s biggest DJs collaborating on F1 Tracks – the official F1 playlist – or huge names like Diplo performing at this year’s Singapore Grand Prix. The crossover between passions is clear, and who knows? Perhaps another driver will take up DJing after retirement – much like Alonso's compatriot Jaime Alguersuari, who now goes by the stage name Squire.

title: 10 unexpected careers F1 drivers pursued away from the track
excerpt:
For Formula 1 drivers, retirement does not necessarily mean leaving the sport behind. Plenty swap the cockpit for the commentary box, while others become team bosses, ambassadors or driver managers – keeping one foot firmly planted in the paddock.

But for some, life away from F1 has taken a rather different turn. Across the decades, former drivers have traded racing cars for everything from fishing trawlers and farms to DJ decks and even political office.

Here are 10 F1 drivers whose careers away from the track took them somewhere rather unexpected...

Niki Lauda – Airline entrepreneur

There aren't many things Niki Lauda didn't accomplish in Formula 1. The Austrian won three World Championships across two spells in the sport, famously battled James Hunt for the 1976 World Championship and eventually returned to the paddock in senior roles with Ferrari, Jaguar and Mercedes.

But even while his driving career was still unfolding, Lauda had another fascination entirely – aviation. He established Lauda Air in 1979, the same year he first stepped away from F1, and began building what would eventually become an international airline operating long-haul services around the world. After returning to Formula 1 with McLaren in 1982 and claiming a third World Championship, he retired for good three years later and turned his attention to aviation full-time, later expanding his involvement with ventures such as Niki and Laudamotion.

Being a three-time World Champion and playing a major role in Mercedes' future dominance would probably constitute enough careers for most people. But Lauda somehow found time to become a successful airline entrepreneur as well.

Paolo Barilla – Pasta executive

Paolo Barilla's time in Formula 1 was relatively brief. The Italian made his debut for Minardi at the 1989 Japanese Grand Prix and went on to enter 15 Grands Prix across two seasons, starting nine of them and recording a best finish of 11th. His racing CV extended well beyond F1, however – most notably including an outright victory at the 24 Hours of Le Mans in 1985.

By 1991, Barilla was ready for something different. Fortunately, there was a rather famous family business waiting for him.

He joined Barilla France before being appointed Deputy Chairman of the Barilla Group in 1994, a position he continues to hold. More than three decades after leaving the F1 grid, his two careers even collided when Barilla became an official Formula 1 partner in 2025.

Speaking at the announcement, Barilla said: “A lightning-fast F1 car and a delicious plate of pasta: what do they have in common? At first, it may not be obvious, but behind both, and the effort that goes into making them, are skilled professionals, passionate and determined, driven by the desire to keep improving.”

Perhaps racing cars and pasta have more in common than first meets the eye...

Carlos Reutemann – Politician

Carlos Reutemann came agonisingly close to becoming an F1 World Champion, losing the 1981 title to Nelson Piquet by a single point after arriving at the season finale in Las Vegas at the top of the standings.

By the time he stepped away from F1 in 1982, the Argentine had accumulated 12 Grand Prix victories and established himself as one of his country's greatest drivers behind five-time champion Juan Manuel Fangio. After briefly returning to rallying, Reutemann then entered an arena that could arguably be every bit as competitive as Formula 1 – politics.

In 1991, he was elected governor of his home province of Santa Fe, serving until 1995 before returning for a second term between 1999 and 2003. He then moved into Argentina's National Senate, winning re-election in both 2009 and 2015 and remaining a senator until his death in 2021.

Reutemann's political profile grew so significantly that he was considered a serious potential candidate for the Argentine presidency – but declined to run in 2002. From fighting for the F1 title to potentially fighting for the country's highest office, his competitive career certainly didn't end at the chequered flag.

Alex Ribeiro – Sports chaplain

Anyone familiar with Alex Ribeiro's racing cars might not be too surprised by the direction his life eventually took.

The Brazilian competed in F1 during the 1970s for Hesketh, March and Copersucar-Fittipaldi, but became just as recognisable for the enormous 'Jesus Saves' message carried on his F2 racing machinery. His Christian faith was an important part of his identity throughout his career and became an even bigger part of his life after leaving F1.

Ribeiro became heavily involved with the organisation Atletas de Cristo – Athletes of Christ – supporting sportspeople across Brazil and serving as its executive director. His work took him far beyond motorsport, with Ribeiro acting as a chaplain to Christian members of the Brazilian national football team across several World Cups, including the victorious 1994 campaign in the United States.

Remarkably, his second career even brought him back into the F1 paddock. Ribeiro later drove the sport's Medical Car while also carrying out chaplaincy work – meaning that even decades after his Grand Prix career ended, he found a very different way to continue helping athletes at the highest level.

Jaime Alguersuari – DJ and producer

When Jaime Alguersuari made his F1 debut for Toro Rosso at the 2009 Hungarian Grand Prix, the 19-year-old became the youngest driver the sport had ever seen at that point.

But just a few years later, his life looked completely different. After losing his Toro Rosso seat at the end of 2011, Alguersuari continued competing in categories including Formula E and GT racing. However, his passion for motorsport gradually disappeared and, still only in his mid-20s, the Spaniard decided to walk away from racing entirely.

Fortunately, another passion had been developing alongside it. Alguersuari had been producing electronic music even during his F1 career and eventually turned his attention to it full-time under the name Squire, a nod to his second surname, Escudero. He has since released music and performed internationally as a DJ and producer.

Plenty of drivers have talked about needing to find a new rhythm after leaving Formula 1. Alguersuari took that rather more literally.

Jody Scheckter – Farmer

Jody Scheckter's F1 career ended with one of the ultimate achievements already secured. The South African won the 1979 World Championship with Ferrari before retiring from the sport after one final season with the Scuderia in 1980.

His first move away from racing was already somewhat unconventional. Scheckter built a successful firearms training technology business in the United States – but even that would eventually give way to another dramatic change of direction…farming.

Scheckter established Laverstoke Park Farm in Hampshire, developing thousands of acres around natural and biodynamic farming principles. The operation became home to sheep, cattle and a particularly sizeable population of water buffalo, whose milk was used to make mozzarella. The farm also produced everything from meat and ice cream to sparkling wine.

Jacques Villeneuve – Singer-songwriter

Jacques Villeneuve achieved more than most racing drivers could dream of before turning 27. He won the Indianapolis 500 and CART title in 1995, arrived in Formula 1 the following year and became World Champion with Williams in just his second season.

But Villeneuve had another creative interest bubbling away in the background. He had been writing lyrics and playing guitar for years, and after his final F1 appearance in 2006 he was finally able to give music rather more attention.

The result was Private Paradise, a 13-track acoustic album released in 2007 featuring songs in both French and English. Villeneuve wrote six of the tracks himself, including Father, which paid tribute to his late father and Ferrari legend Gilles Villeneuve.

It would be fair to say that Villeneuve's musical career never quite reached the heights of his racing one – Private Paradise did not exactly trouble the upper reaches of the charts. But how many F1 World Champions can say they followed up a title-winning racing career by releasing a bilingual acoustic-rock album?

Alex Zanardi – Paralympic champion

Alex Zanardi's journey after Formula 1 is unlike any other on this list.

The Italian raced in F1 across the 1990s, but enjoyed his greatest success in America, becoming a two-time CART champion in 1997 and 1998. In 2001, during a CART race at the Lausitzring in Germany, Zanardi suffered a devastating accident which resulted in the loss of both of his legs.

Remarkably, his racing career did not end there. Zanardi returned to competitive motorsport with adapted controls before discovering handcycling – initially taking part in marathons before setting his sights on the Paralympic Games.

At London 2012 he won two individual gold medals at Brands Hatch, a circuit where he had raced more than two decades earlier, along with silver in the team relay. Four years later in Rio, he added another two golds and a silver to take his career Paralympic tally to six medals.

Zanardi, who passed away in May 2026 at the age of 59, became one of the most decorated Para cyclists of his generation.

Stefan Johansson – Artist

Stefan Johansson's racing career took him almost everywhere. The Swede drove for Ferrari and McLaren in Formula 1, competed in IndyCar and eventually won the 24 Hours of Le Mans in 1997.

But alongside all that racing, Johansson had quietly begun developing a very different skill.

He started painting in 1986 after the death of his close friend and fellow F1 driver Elio de Angelis and has since explained that painting helped him process the experience.

After stepping back from driving, Johansson channelled more of his energy into art and design. His work has often drawn directly from racing – including abstract pieces designed to capture the sensation of speed, paintings of moments from his own career and even an art car based around a Porsche fitted with an F1-derived TAG turbo engine.

Innes Ireland – Commercial fisherman

Innes Ireland was never likely to choose a particularly conventional retirement.

As a former paratrooper and engineer before reaching Formula 1, Ireland became one of the sport's great characters during the late 1950s and 1960s. He also earned a significant place in Lotus history when he won the 1961 United States Grand Prix at Watkins Glen International – the team's first World Championship Grand Prix victory.

After his racing career wound down, Ireland returned to Scotland and swapped racing cars for fishing boats. Based around Kirkcudbright, he operated trawlers and went out to sea himself, with local records showing that he bought and refitted an ageing Norwegian trawler called Vetrung as well as another Norwegian vessel which he converted for lobster fishing.

But despite the dramatic change of machinery, some old habits apparently remained. When a well-known motorsport magazine visited Ireland in the 1970s, he arrived back from a fishing expedition and proceeded to spin his boat twice in the narrow harbour as the journalists watched from shore.

Different vehicle, same Innes Ireland.

Honorary mention: Nigel Mansell – Member of the Magic Circle

Nigel Mansell might not have turned magic into a second career, but the 1992 World Champion did take the hobby seriously enough to become a member of The Magic Circle – one of the world’s most prestigious societies for magicians.

Mansell took up magic later in life and has spoken about how learning tricks helped challenge and retrain his brain, eventually earning his place in the famous society after demonstrating his skills.

Not quite a career change – but becoming a bona fide member of The Magic Circle is a pretty impressive retirement hobby.

title: 7 times a stellar performance helped a driver bounce back
excerpt:
There were plenty of talking points to emerge from the final Dutch Grand Prix, but a key one involved the return of Yuki Tsunoda and his determined drive at the wheel of the Racing Bulls machine.

Having lost his seat at Red Bull following a tricky 2025 season, Tsunoda had been on the sidelines as a test and reserve driver – but the Japanese racer took the opportunity to show what he could do when standing in for Liam Lawson, who in turn had been called up to substitute for an injured Isack Hadjar at the main team.

“I did everything I could today and I really enjoyed it,” Tsunoda said after just missing out on points in P11. It remains to be seen if it will be enough to secure the 26-year-old a full-time return to the grid, but he may well take heart from these past instances of drivers who bounced back following an eye-catching performance…

Nico Hulkenberg

One name who finished just a few positions ahead of Tsunoda in Zandvoort was Nico Hulkenberg, a driver who knows all too well about the impact that a solid stand-in drive can have.

After being left without a seat at the end of 2019 when he was dropped by Renault, Hulkenberg made not one but three substitute appearances for Racing Point during the 2020 campaign when Sergio Perez and Lance Stroll each contracted Covid-19.

While he was unable to start his first outing at Silverstone due to an issue with his car, the German seized his second chance during the 70th Anniversary Grand Prix at the same venue one week later, taking third place on the grid behind the Mercedes cars before ending the race in P7.

His third ‘super-sub’ run at the Nurburgring saw him climb from the back of the field to eighth place, leading Racing Point to sign him as their official reserve for 2021 – a move that kept him in the minds of those in the paddock and, after two more stand-in weekends during 2022, arguably helped Hulkenberg to secure a full-time comeback with Haas in 2023.

The 39-year-old has since continued to thrive, having gone on to join the then-called Kick Sauber outfit – now Audi – last season where he scored a long-awaited maiden podium at the British Grand Prix.

Carlos Sainz

Unlike Tsunoda and Hulkenberg, Carlos Sainz has not yet found himself on the sidelines in Formula 1 – but the Spaniard did enter the 2024 campaign in the unusual position of already knowing that he would be leaving his team at the end of the year.

The blockbuster news during the winter that Lewis Hamilton would switch from Mercedes to Ferrari in 2025 took many by surprise – perhaps including Sainz, who would be the driver stepping aside at the Scuderia for the seven-time World Champion.

To make matters worse, the man from Madrid was forced to sit out Round 2 in Saudi Arabia after undergoing surgery for appendicitis, leading to then-F2 racer Ollie Bearman stepping in for a memorable substitute appearance of his own.

Sainz returned to action only two weeks later at the Australian Grand Prix and embarked on an incredible comeback performance, claiming second on the grid before taking his third career victory.

It was a remarkable story and acted as a reminder of Sainz’s skills, with the Spanish racer subsequently targeted by several teams for a 2025 seat. He would eventually go on to sign for Williams later in the year.

Alain Prost

Another name who had to find a way to bounce back after parting ways with Ferrari – albeit in a far more acrimonious fashion – was Alain Prost.

Following his switch from McLaren, Prost’s maiden campaign with the Scuderia in 1990 ended with him missing out on the title in controversial fashion to long-time rival Ayrton Senna.

Tensions started to build between the Frenchman and his team during 1991, with Prost publicly criticising Ferrari following their drop in competitiveness – and the then three-time World Champion was axed by the Italian outfit before the season was over.

With no time left to find a suitable seat for 1992, Prost was forced to take a sabbatical – but the driver known as ‘the Professor’ had not finished with F1 yet and returned to the grid with Williams for the 1993 season.

The potential of the partnership was clear from the offset as Prost converted pole position into victory at his first race back behind the wheel in South Africa. It set the tone for the rest of the championship, as from there onwards the French driver collected six further victories en route to his fourth title before retiring at the end of the campaign.

Mika Salo

While Prost bowed out of Formula 1 prior to 1994, that season would see Mika Salo make his debut towards the end of the championship for the Lotus team. The Finn went on to race for Tyrrell and Arrows in the years that followed, but was left without a seat in 1999.

However, an opportunity to return arose when he stood in for an injured Ricardo Zonta at BAR for three races – before an even bigger call-up came when Ferrari brought in Salo to replace Michael Schumacher for several rounds after the German broke his leg in a crash at Silverstone.

Despite having some illustrious shoes to fill, Salo acquitted himself well with a P9 finish on his first outing in Austria – but it was at Germany’s Hockenheim circuit one round later where the Finnish driver really caught the eye.

Salo lined up in fourth on the grid and went on to find himself in the lead of the race, before moving aside for team mate Eddie Irvine who was fighting McLaren’s Mika Hakkinen for the World Championship. Finishing P2 still marked Salo’s best career result and maiden F1 podium.

After another four appearances for Ferrari – which included a second rostrum at Monza – Salo’s contributions helped the squad to seal the Teams’ Championship, while his performances also impressed Sauber who signed him for a full-time return in 2000.

Valtteri Bottas

Another ‘flying Finn’ to have been through something of a relaunch is Valtteri Bottas. After experiencing a solid first season as a Mercedes driver in 2017 – during which he scored his maiden F1 victory – a winless 2018 campaign saw Bottas slip back to fifth in the standings, all while team mate Lewis Hamilton surged to a sixth World Championship.

Bottas later revealed that he considered walking away from the sport off the back of such a challenging year, having fallen into a “dark place” – but the Finnish racer instead took the opportunity to regroup during the winter and come back stronger for 2019.

That goal was one he aced at the first race of the campaign in Australia. After lining up behind polesitter Hamilton on the grid, Bottas overtook his team mate into the first corner and went on to claim a dominant win with a sizeable 20-second margin.

His return to the top prompted ‘Bottas 2.0’ to famously remark over the radio, “To whom it may concern, f*** you!”, a comment that he later admitted was “just all the frustration from the year before coming out”.

That performance marked the beginning of the Finn’s strongest season to date in Formula 1, during which he clinched four victories and ended the campaign in second place of the Drivers’ Championship.

As Bottas knows, a strong comeback performance can be the ultimate way to bounce back from a tough spell – or, in the case of Kevin Magnussen, mark a memorable return to the grid after a year away.

The Dane subsequently turned his attentions to other categories of motorsport for the next year – before receiving a late call-up from Haas to replace Mazepin for the 2022 season, an opportunity that he accepted.

Despite his time away from the sport, Magnussen was promptly back up to speed at the first race in Bahrain and qualified an impressive seventh on the grid. He then turned this into a P5 result on race day, leading then-Team Principal Guenther Steiner to famously remark that it was “some f****** Viking comeback”.

There were further celebrations in store for Magnussen and Haas later in the year when he scored a surprise pole position in Sao Paulo. The partnership continued on until the end of 2024, with Magnussen having since returned to other series such as the World Endurance Championship.

Sergio Perez

Sergio Perez has enjoyed an extensive F1 career since his debut for Sauber in 2011, the Mexican going on to race with McLaren for one season in 2013 before moving to Force India in the campaign that followed.

However, after remaining with the team over the course of the next few years, Perez was suddenly faced with an uncertain future when four-time World Champion Sebastian Vettel signed to the squad ahead of their rebrand as Aston Martin for 2021, leaving him without a seat.

It did not take long for the driver from Guadalajara to put himself in the shop window following the news, going on to claim a P2 finish for the then-named Racing Point outfit in Turkiye – but even better was to come two rounds later in Sakhir.

Amid an eventful race – in which he slipped to the back of the field following a first-lap incident – Perez embarked on a notable recovery drive en route to a maiden F1 victory, making him the first Mexican driver to win a race since Pedro Rodriguez in 1970.

That performance doubtless helped Perez’s case as he fought for a spot on the 2021 grid, with Red Bull later signing him up to kickstart what would go on to be a four-year run at the championship-winning team.

title: Tsolov completes first F1 test with Racing Bulls
excerpt:
Formula 2 championship leader and Red Bull junior Nikola Tsolov has taken part in his first F1 test for Racing Bulls at the Autodromo Internazionale Enzo e Dino Ferrari – better known to many as Imola – in Italy.

Tsolov completed 690km as part of a Testing of Previous Cars (TPC) programme, a milestone moment for the 19-year-old as he continues his development with the Red Bull Junior Programme.

“First TPC day in a Formula 1 car done, and I’m super happy with how today went,” Tsolov said after the experience. “I really enjoyed every lap and it’s difficult to put into words what it means to finally get this opportunity.

“A massive thank you to VCARB and the Red Bull Junior Team for believing in me and giving me this opportunity. It’s something I’ve been working towards my whole life, so to finally experience it is pretty incredible.

“I still don’t think I’ve fully comprehended what we achieved today, but I enjoyed every lap and hopefully I’ll get the chance to add some more kilometres soon.”

Alan Permane, Team Principal at Racing Bulls, added: “Today was a really positive step for Nikola. He adapted quickly to the car and showed the composure you want to see from a driver taking on an F1 car for the first time.

“The outing is part of the ongoing development plan the team runs for its junior drivers, giving them the tools, the mileage, and the environment to develop. We've seen time and again what this pathway can produce, and it’s days like today that are part of how we keep building it."

Tsolov – who currently leads the F2 standings by 20 points from Gabriele Mini – has seen his name mentioned in speculation over Racing Bulls’ line-up for the 2027 F1 season, with Permane commenting in July: “It’s not an untruth to say we’re not thinking about it at the moment.

“He's there, he’s doing his job, we're doing our job, and we'll make a call if and when he comes up to Racing Bulls later this year.”

The focus for Tsolov currently remains on the Formula 2 championship fight, however, which will continue next weekend at Monza.

title: Guenther Steiner claims Mercedes has made George Russell's support role clear
excerpt:
Former Haas Formula 1 team principal Guenther Steiner believes Mercedes will have informed George Russell that his role for the remainder of the 2026 season is to support Kimi Antonelli's championship campaign.

While Russell arrived at the season-opening Australian Grand Prix as a clear favourite for the 2026 drivers' title, his team-mate became the youngest driver to lead the standings after back-to-back wins at the Chinese and Japanese Grands Prix.

In the first half of the season, Russell won two grands prix and Antonelli won six. The Italian currently leads with 242 points, while Russell is second on 183 points, level with Lewis Hamilton.

The 28-year-old was asked to allow Antonelli through during the Dutch Grand Prix, a decision that has once again raised questions about the team dynamics, despite team chief Toto Wolff claiming the instruction had nothing to do with the championship.

Russell briefly questioned the instruction over team radio before allowing his team-mate to pass. Russell, who finished third behind race winner Lando Norris and Antonelli, confirmed to the media after the race that it was the right choice, as his team-mate would likely have passed him anyway on fresher tyres.

Andrea Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes, George Russell, Mercedes

Photo by: Simon Galloway / LAT Images via Getty Images

Speaking on The Red Flags Podcast, Steiner suggested that a clear conversation must have taken place over the summer break to establish the new rules of engagement, although this has not been confirmed by the team or drivers.

"I wouldn't say they told him, 'You're the number two driver.' They told him, 'You are now here to support Kimi.' I wouldn't call him the number two driver, but, 'If needed, you need to support Kimi to win the world championship. This is your mission for this season.' No, I think that happened," Steiner explained.

"If you want to win, this is what you have to do. Otherwise, you take the risk as McLaren did last year, then get down to the last race to lose that world championship, not to win it, to lose it."

title: Audi F1 power unit facility branded "second to none" by Rob Smedley
excerpt:
Former Ferrari race engineer Rob Smedley has lauded Audi's Formula 1 power unit headquarters, declaring the German manufacturer's engine department as "second to none".

Speaking on the High Performance Racing podcast alongside host Jake Humphrey and former Alpine team principal Otmar Szafnauer, Smedley evaluated the grid's progress in the first half of the season.

While Audi has faced a steep learning curve since taking over the Sauber operation and becoming a works outfit, Smedley pointed to the scale and quality of its powertrain investment.

"Sauber, I mean, they were pretty desperate these last two or three years. They were just awful, there's no other word for it," the former engineer said.

When Szafnauer argued that Audi still owned the team at that stage, so it had good financial backing and decent infrastructure, Smedley added: "They've always had a very good wind tunnel, or have for a long time. But now, if you look at their facility in Germany, the engine facility, the power unit facility, that is second to none, and they're still building and still going on it.

Nico Hülkenberg, Audi

Photo by: Eric Le Galliot

"So, this is a huge project for them. Hinwil as a Formula 1 facility leaves maybe a little bit to be desired. But they're expanding that, and there are plans of where they want to go with it. So, this is a really important project for them."

Audi retained the 2025 Sauber driver line-up of Nico Hulkenberg and Gabriel Bortoleto. After 12 rounds of the 2026 season, the team sits eighth in the constructors' championship with 16 points. Bortoleto is 14th in the drivers' standings with 10 points and Hulkenberg is 15th with six points.

title: Sergio Perez "had conversations" with other F1 teams - but never thought of leaving Cadillac
excerpt:
Sergio Perez revealed that his management had held talks with other Formula 1 teams about a potential 2027 switch, but he wants to remain part of Cadillac to help drive the team forward.

It had been rumoured that Perez's management team had been in discussions with Williams about a drive, should Carlos Sainz have elected to leave the team. Sainz then signed a multi-year extension with the Grove outfit, closing off that potential avenue.

Perez has also been linked with the likes of Alpine, but the team will stick with Franco Colapinto for 2027 as the Argentine's performances have improved over the course of his first full year at the Enstone outfit.

Regardless, the Mexican driver told Formula 1's Beyond the Grid podcast that he is fully committed to the Cadillac project and wants to continue to help with the growth of the American squad beyond its debut season.

"For me, nothing has changed," he said. "Of course, we've had conversations with other teams and here and there, a few teams have been calling and stuff, but for me, nothing has changed.

"I see this as my project and I want to be part of Cadillac. I really believe [in it].

"I don't think this is a one-year project. I think this is a long-term project that I want to be part of. Obviously, there will be some discussions, but this is where I want to be and nothing has changed from my side."

Sergio Perez, Cadillac Racing

Photo by: Guido De Bortoli / LAT Images via Getty Images

Perez added that he wished to see the team improve, and was keen to the impact of new team principal Marcin Budkowski on the team. Budkowski took over from Graeme Lowdon, as the Northumbrian was let go by Cadillac during the summer break.

Speaking about what Cadillac needed to do to improve, Perez explained that it was not simply a performance-related pursuit, but how the team works operationally to get on top of pitstops, strategy, and other aspects laid out by the track team.

"I want to see more progress. Closing out the gap to the teams ahead of us," he said. "I don't know who's ahead at the moment, I don't know if it's Williams, Aston seems to have become part [of the midfield] and being able to mix with them more in the races.

"Being able to close that gap will only allow us to start next year in a much better shape. And that's something I want to see. Obviously, I'm looking forward to work with Marcin and see his leadership.

"I think there's a lot of room for improvement. Not just on performance, operationally, pitstops, strategy, tyres.

"There's so much still - we've only done the 11th race in our history. So there's a lot of things. But I want to see much more progress. Closing out the gap and then I think that will give us a massive boost to start next year."

title: Isack Hadjar shares injury update as he targets Italian GP Red Bull return
excerpt:
Red Bull driver Isack Hadjar is "hopeful" that he will be able to return to the Formula 1 grid for the Italian Grand Prix after a wrist injury forced him to sit out the Dutch Grand Prix.

Hadjar sustained the injury during the summer shutdown. Despite missing Zandvoort's final F1 race, the driver shared that he was "healing fast" while filming with the Milton Keynes outfit last weekend.

While Racing Bulls driver Liam Lawson stepped up to take his place alongside four-time champion Max Verstappen, Hadjar was still present at Zandvoort.

"Actually, it's my first injury ever in my whole existence, career, whatever," he told Red Bull in a behind-the-scenes video of the final Dutch Grand Prix.

"It's weird to be on the bench and I'm not happy about it, for me and for the team. Obviously, I want to be there every lap."

Pointing out his braced wrist, he added: "It's not swollen, which is very good. It's a good sign. So, actually, it's healing fast. Every day I have a bit more mobility and I'm hopeful for Monza."

Standing in for Hadjar, Lawson picked up six points for Red Bull with a seventh-place finish at Zandvoort.

"As for Liam, it's never easy to jump from one team to another," team principal Laurent Mekies said. "Today he took the points that we were able to take. Yesterday, he did a very good job in qualifying, being very close to Max and we thank him for having been able to adapt so quickly to the team."

The Italian Grand Prix at Monza will take place from 4-6 September. At this stage, neither Red Bull nor Hadjar has officially confirmed whether he will be back in the cockpit in Italy.

Hadjar currently sits eighth in the drivers' standings with 68 points. His team-mate Verstappen is sixth with 112 points.

title: Haas completes latest TPC test as focus on 2027 F1 driver line-up decision grows
excerpt:
Haas has completed its latest Testing of Previous Cars (TPC) run with Ryo Hirakawa, Leonardo Fornaroli and Rafael Camara in action, as focus on its 2027 Formula 1 driver line-up increases.

With the 2027 F1 silly season picking up speed since the end of the summer break, Haas is one of the few teams to officially decide its driver line-up for next season.

While Oliver Bearman looks assured of retaining his place at the team for 2027, attention has turned to Esteban Ocon’s position, with Haas making no secret of its intention to assess all of its options.

The American team has just completed a three-day TPC test at Portimao, where reserve driver Hirakawa was in action alongside 2025 Formula 2 champion and McLaren development driver Fornaroli and current F2 title contender and Ferrari junior Camara. Each driver completed laps in the VF-25 – Haas’ 2025 F1 car – at the Portuguese venue from 26-28 August.

It follows a similar TPC test Haas ran last month, when it gave an opportunity to Toyota-backed drivers Sho Tsuboi and Nirei Fukuzumi at Fuji.

While no further information has been revealed about the Portimao TPC test, it was made clear it was part of the wider plan by Haas to evaluate all interested drivers before making a final decision on its 2027 line-up.

Ayao Komatsu, Haas F1 Team

Photo by: Simon Galloway / LAT Images via Getty Images

“I think it's really good that other people are actually interested in us,” Haas team principal Ayao Komatsu said ahead of the Dutch GP last weekend.

“At the moment, we're not performing so well. We cannot challenge for points, but I think it's nice that other people can see the potential in us. Within the constraint how we're fighting and we're trying to improve the team. We just take it as a compliment that other drivers are interested.”

Komatsu has stressed his immediate focus is on the short term to maximise performance from both the car and its drivers in 2026, indicating Haas will take its time to decide its future driver pairing.

In Haas’ short history in F1, it has often been one of the last teams to announce its driver line-up for the following season – so a similar timeline isn’t unrealistic given the relatively stable driver line-ups elsewhere on the grid for 2027.

“We’re not in any rush,” Komatsu said at Zandvoort. “We’re focused on our two drivers, Ollie and Esteban, trying to get the best out of them. They’ve got the tough challenge, right? You know what they are capable of.

“Ollie has showed it repeatedly, Esteban, when he is happy with the car, you know what he can do. So we need to really just focus on providing them with the best possible car, best set-up adaptation, and get the best out of them. And then both of our drivers are fully focused. So at the moment, we’re focused on that.”

title: What Norris' contract extension means for McLaren and Piastri
excerpt:
With what is undoubtedly coming with a salary befitting a world champion, Lando Norris has put pen to paper to a deal tying him to the Woking-based team until 2030, with options for multiple additional years after that, taking Norris into his 30s.

Imagining Norris wearing a different-coloured race suit has always felt like a mind-bending exercise. Now, the 26-year-old's bumper McLaren contract has definitively taken one of F1's leading stars out of the driver market for years to come, turning Norris into a bona fide franchise driver for the team.

Read Also:

Formula 1Norris extends McLaren deal until F1 2030

Norris started his McLaren career a decade ago, when he was picked up by Zak Brown and supported through the single-seater ranks with Carlin, replacing Stoffel Vandoorne as a grand prix driver in 2019 as part of a new wave of Britain-born talent including George Russell and Alex Albon.

Turning from a fast but raw and insecure talent into a championship-winning superstar, last season was undoubtedly Norris' coming-of-age year, overcoming driving style struggles, mechanical failures and a formidable team-mate in Oscar Piastri to take his first world championship.

That triumph seems to have changed something within Norris. From hoping he could one day achieve his dreams, he finally gained the confidence to know that he could. Seeing is believing.

"Lando is driving and operating at the level of a world champion," team boss Andrea Stella said after Norris' Zandvoort win. "What I like the most about his journey in Formula 1 is that he keeps improving. And I think especially after the start of the 2025 season, something clicked, which is not only a single click, but is a way of working with Lando and that we are adopting also on Oscar's side now in particular. And I think this approach has led Lando to continuous improvements."

Andrea Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes, Lando Norris, McLaren

Photo by: Alastair Staley / LAT Images via Getty Images

Search for stability underpins quiet 2027 silly season

It's exactly the type of steady presence, then, that McLaren was keen to tie down for the foreseeable future, willing to fork out an undisclosed but no doubt significant chunk of cash to do so.

Aged 26, Norris is only just entering his prime, so securing its most successful driver since Lewis Hamilton provides McLaren with additional stability as it aims to overcome a slow-ish start to the 2026 season. Norris' brace of wins either side of the summer break are a sign the team is starting to get there.

One look at a particularly quiet transfer market further reinforces the idea that stability is a prized quality to have right now. Teams have been stretched to their limits with the complex 2026 power unit regulations, so they are keen to remove as many unknowns off the board elsewhere, as long as their drivers are performing.

When Max Verstappen, as ever the silly season's dominant domino, decided to stay put at Red Bull, the 2027 starting grid was inevitably going to look very similar to this year's. Alongside Verstappen's decade-long tenure at the Milton Keynes team, Charles Leclerc has also reinforced his commitment to Ferrari, and Mercedes will no doubt want to achieve the same longevity with its drivers, especially Kimi Antonelli.

Speaking to Motorsport.com, Ferrari team boss Fred Vasseur explained the value of Leclerc's long-term relationship with Maranello: "Having this kind of continuity is always positive. For me it's also much easier to work with drivers that I have known for ages. Sometimes you don't need to discuss [something] when you have known someone for 10, 15 or 20 years, when the first feeling is the good one, and you know what he's thinking."

It is clear that mutual trust and understanding also exists between Norris and McLaren, to the benefit of both parties.

Oscar Piastri, McLaren

Photo by: Pauline Ballet / LAT Images via Getty Images

What about Piastri?

It will be intriguing to see how Piastri and his camp look at this high-profile deal for his team-mate. The Australian extended his deal to 2028 at the start of the 2025 championship, which looked like his to lose until a combination of a decline in performance, driver mistakes, team errors and bad luck saw him finish behind both Norris and Verstappen.

It was a huge blow to Piastri, and unease over team orders and the team's rules of engagement at points through the 2025 campaign, such as a controversial position swap at the Italian Grand Prix or contact between the two team-mates in Singapore and Austin, may well replay on his or his management's mind when digesting the implications of Norris' long-term big money deal. Those who believe McLaren is and always will be Norris' team certainly won't see his contract extension as anything other than a confirmation of that idea.

But right now, Piastri has more pressing concerns. Compared to his ironclad first half of the 2025 season, the 25-year-old has suffered an extended slump in performance with the 2026 generation of cars, seemingly going through similar driving style struggles that he faced last year on low-grip circuits like Austin and Mexico.

Read Also:

Formula 1Why Piastri is struggling to match Norris – and McLaren’s intriguing explanation

Team principal Stella said Piastri's issues are "purely technical" rather than anything mental, whether related to how 2025 finished or 2026 started, as he reaches a full calendar year without a grand prix win on Monday.

McLaren's solution isn't too dissimilar to how it fixed Norris last year, working with Piastri behind the scenes to make adaptations both from a car and driving style point of view. If it succeeds, it has its two aces back for what is shaping up to be a closely-fought second half of 2026, and a potential title challenge next year.

McLaren's end goal is still for both drivers to be fighting each other for wins and titles, which would involve Piastri following a similar trajectory towards a long-term contract extension. It is up to the Australian's camp to decide whether that's in his interest, or whether it might be time to explore new horizons. In any case, Piastri's current deal until the end of 2028 means time is on his side. The same can be said for McLaren.

In the meantime, McLaren has its reigning world champion tied up for the entirety of the current rules cycle. It's one less puzzle piece on the board as the Woking squad aims to retain and even reinforce its title-winning team.

When Max Verstappen, as ever the silly season's dominant domino, decided to stay put at Red Bull, the 2027 starting grid was inevitably going to look very similar to this year's. Alongside Verstappen's decade-long tenure at the Milton Keynes team, Charles Leclerc has also reinforced his commitment to Ferrari, and Mercedes will no doubt want to achieve the same longevity with its drivers, especially Kimi Antonelli.

Speaking to Motorsport.com, Ferrari team boss Fred Vasseur explained the value of Leclerc's long-term relationship with Maranello: "Having this kind of continuity is always positive. For me it's also much easier to work with drivers that I have known for ages. Sometimes you don't need to discuss [something] when you have known someone for 10, 15 or 20 years, when the first feeling is the good one, and you know what he's thinking."

It is clear that mutual trust and understanding also exists between Norris and McLaren, to the benefit of both parties.

Oscar Piastri, McLaren

Photo by: Pauline Ballet / LAT Images via Getty Images

What about Piastri?

It will be intriguing to see how Piastri and his camp look at this high-profile deal for his team-mate. The Australian extended his deal to 2028 at the start of the 2025 championship, which looked like his to lose until a combination of a decline in performance, driver mistakes, team errors and bad luck saw him finish behind both Norris and Verstappen.

It was a huge blow to Piastri, and unease over team orders and the team's rules of engagement at points through the 2025 campaign, such as a controversial position swap at the Italian Grand Prix or contact between the two team-mates in Singapore and Austin, may well replay on his or his management's mind when digesting the implications of Norris' long-term big money deal. Those who believe McLaren is and always will be Norris' team certainly won't see his contract extension as anything other than a confirmation of that idea.

But right now, Piastri has more pressing concerns. Compared to his ironclad first half of the 2025 season, the 25-year-old has suffered an extended slump in performance with the 2026 generation of cars, seemingly going through similar driving style struggles that he faced last year on low-grip circuits like Austin and Mexico.

Team principal Stella said Piastri's issues are "purely technical" rather than anything mental, whether related to how 2025 finished or 2026 started, as he reaches a full calendar year without a grand prix win on Monday.

McLaren's solution isn't too dissimilar to how it fixed Norris last year, working with Piastri behind the scenes to make adaptations both from a car and driving style point of view. If it succeeds, it has its two aces back for what is shaping up to be a closely-fought second half of 2026, and a potential title challenge next year.

McLaren's end goal is still for both drivers to be fighting each other for wins and titles, which would involve Piastri following a similar trajectory towards a long-term contract extension. It is up to the Australian's camp to decide whether that's in his interest, or whether it might be time to explore new horizons. In any case, Piastri's current deal until the end of 2028 means time is on his side. The same can be said for McLaren.

title: Ferrari urged to back Lewis Hamilton as Guenther Steiner issues team order warning
excerpt:
Former Haas Formula 1 team principal Guenther Steiner believes Ferrari must establish clear rules of engagement and back Lewis Hamilton over Charles Leclerc if the Maranello outfit wants to stay in the 2026 championship fight.

Ferrari's internal dynamic came under scrutiny after the Dutch Grand Prix at Zandvoort, where contrasting strategies led to friction between the drivers. Hamilton, running on fresher tyres and showing stronger pace, was held up behind Leclerc. The delay cost the seven-time champion and prompted frustrated radio complaints.

Speaking on The Red Flags Podcast, Steiner argued that Ferrari failed to prepare its drivers for potential team orders before the race.

"You cannot implement team orders during a race," Steiner explained. "You need to agree them beforehand. The realistic thing is, can Charles really win the world championship? Maybe not. And who is in front? Lewis.

"I haven't done the calculations of how realistic it is for him to win the world championship, but if one of the two can win, it is Lewis. So, as somebody else has shown, if you want to win, it's very tight up front there. You need to put your money on the guy who has got the better chance.

title: Norris extends McLaren deal until F1 2030
excerpt:
Lando Norris and McLaren have agreed to a long-term contract extension, keeping the world champion at the Formula 1 team until at least 2030.

On Saturday morning McLaren announced it had tied Norris to the team until 2030, with multi-year options to further extend the 26-year-old's stay. Norris personally announced the news to the Woking factory staff during the team's annual family and friends open day.

"McLaren is my home, and I’m very pleased to be signing a new contract to keep me with the team until at least 2030," Norris said. "When I started this journey nine years ago, I was clear about the goals I wanted to achieve: to get McLaren back to the front and to win championships.

"We’ve achieved that goal, but we want more, we want to keep on winning, and we know as a team that we’re capable of achieving it. I can’t wait to get back in the car in Monza and I’m very excited about what the future holds for us, both over the rest of this season, and in the coming years.”

Read Also:

Formula 1Why McLaren thinks Norris is even better now than his F1 title-winning year

Norris' previous deal ran until the end of 2027, effectively increasing the Briton's stay at Woking for at least four more years. Team-mate Oscar Piastri is still under contract until the end of 2028 after extending his deal at the start of last year.

Salaries are rarely revealed in F1, but it stands to reason Norris is in line for a bumper pay rise off the back of his world title and his all-round progress as a driver, which has carried through into a strong first half of 2026. Norris capitalised on McLaren's car upgrades to win the last two grands prix in Hungary and the Netherlands.

Lando Norris, McLaren

Photo by: Pauline Ballet - Formula 1

In addition to the new contract extension, Norris was also gifted with his championship-winning 2025 car, the MCL39.

Team principal Andrea Stella was "delighted" to continue working with Norris for the foreseeable future. "He is an exceptional driver, someone who combines outstanding natural speed with maturity, consistency and a strong commitment to McLaren, but above all, he is a special human being who is valued by everyone in the team," Stella said.

"Since joining McLaren as part of our junior programme, he has grown with us and played a central role in bringing the team back to the front of Formula 1. This extension gives us important continuity and reinforces our confidence in the direction we are taking together. With him and Oscar, we know we can count not only on one of the strongest partnerships but also on one of the most united and close-knit teams in Formula 1."

Read Also:

Formula 1‘If you're not ready to adapt, you're not good enough’ - Norris addresses changing driving styles in F1 2026

Norris started his McLaren journey as a junior driver in 2017, before being promoted to a race seat in 2019. He has since exclusively raced for the papaya squad and amassed 13 grand prix wins, 18 poles, and 48 podiums.

The team's CEO Zak Brown, who has played an integral role in bringing Norris through the ranks, said: “His journey with the team is a fantastic example of our commitment to identifying, developing and supporting world-class talent, and his achievements speak for themselves.

"Together with Andrea, Oscar and the wider team, Lando has helped drive McLaren into a new papaya era of success, helping us go from the back of the grid, to double consecutive constructors’ titles in 2024 and 2025 and our first drivers’ championship in 17 years.

"We are extremely excited about what lies ahead and remain fully focused on continuing to compete for wins and championships.”

title: Mercedes still searching for answers on why it was “rubbish” through high-speed corners in Dutch GP
excerpt:
Mercedes trackside engineering director Andrew Shovlin rated the team’s pace through Zandvoort’s high-speed corners as “rubbish” and is looking for answers on its inconsistency between both stints and drivers in the Formula 1 Dutch Grand Prix.

After a strong start to the Zandvoort weekend, with George Russell taking pole and victory in the sprint race, Mercedes dropped behind McLaren’s Lando Norris, who secured pole and victory in the grand prix.

While Mercedes still took 2-3 in qualifying and the race, with Kimi Antonelli getting the better of team-mate Russell in the race to extend his championship lead to 59 points, the team was at a loss on why its early pace didn’t carry through the weekend relative to its main competition.

“We've got a few things on the performance side to try and dig into,” Shovlin said on Mercedes’ Nu Silver Arrows Radio Show. “We're going to be getting on with that this week and see what we learn.

“But there were a few corners where we were pretty rubbish, like that combination of [Turns] 7, 8, 9. You could see [it in] the faster-speed [curves]. And it also gives the tyres on the left-hand side of the car a tough time. And we don't really understand yet fully what's causing that.

“We've got some ideas, but that's not a problem that we've suffered with so far this year. And there's plenty of circuits that have got kind of continued corners in one direction.

“We were a bit off the pace in the fastest of those [turns]. And then our problems kind of grew a bit as we went through. All the other corners look solid.”

James Allison, Mercedes, Andrew Shovlin, Mercedes

Photo by: Sam Bloxham / LAT Images via Getty Images

What added to Mercedes’ confusion was that minimal changes were made to the cars between the sprint race and grand prix, as well as during the race itself. While Shovlin accepts a level of expected pace deviation per tyre compounds and life, seeing each driver suffer at different times during the grand prix left Mercedes uncertain about the cause.

“We didn't change the car. We obviously had different compounds at different stages. But again, we need to understand a bit,” he said.

“George's first stint was a bit lacklustre compared to his later ones. And then with Kimi, first stint was good, and then dropped a bit on the second, dropped a bit more on the third, a bit came back on the third. It wasn't like we were playing around with electronic settings or up and down on flap angles. And for him, the balance of the car was quite different stint on stint.

“The two drivers, normally they report similar things with a car at the end of the race. Both of them, their perception of the balance, and probably the reality is George had a more understeery car, Kimi had a more oversteery car. If we look at how they were set up, we don't yet know quite why we got such a big difference.

Read Also:

“So, though, really good to have a strong point-scoring weekend when we weren't at our best in terms of performance. It was actually good fun, sat on the pitwall and having to make decisions in a hurry. I think the whole team enjoyed that and rose to the occasion. And it was definitely a good result, given where we were.

“But yeah, a bit of head-scratching to do over the next few days.”

As Shovlin pointed out, Mercedes still picked up its second-highest points score as a team this season – 46 points, only behind the 55 points it notched up at the Chinese GP – granted both were sprint race weekends with more points on offer.
